notes.title: V1.1.0 — The Trust Issues Update
notes.description: V1.0 worked. It was alive. It had data, dashboards, and dreams. But it also had the security posture of a house with the front door wide open and a sign that said 'FREE LAPTOPS.' V1.1 is the deadbolt, the alarm system, and the slightly aggressive neighbourhood watch. We went from 'it works' to 'it works and we've thought about what happens when someone tries to make it not work.' Welcome to adulthood.

notes.title: PUT /api/settings Had No Auth. Yes, Really.
notes.description: The endpoint that controls your entire application's settings — the one that changes system behaviour — had zero authentication. None. Not a token. Not a cookie. Not even a polite 'please log in first.' Any human, bot, or particularly ambitious browser extension could have rewritten your app config. We discovered this during the hardening pass and fixed it so fast the commit message was just 'OH NO.' It now requires both authentication AND admin privileges. The door is closed. The deadbolt is on. We've added a chain lock for good measure.

notes.title: 47 Routes Now Have Opinions About Who You Are
notes.description: We added backend permission middleware to 47 write routes across the application. Previously, if you knew the URL, you could POST to it. Create a purchase order? Sure. Delete a lifecycle board entry? Why not. Reassign a project manager? Be our guest. Now every one of these routes checks your role, checks your permissions, and returns a 403 Forbidden with the quiet dignity of a bouncer who doesn't need to explain himself. PO routes, PD routes, weekly reviews, lifecycle transitions, invoice patterns, subcontractor operations, and all Smart Import mutations — all locked down. Your curl commands will need to try harder.

notes.title: Smart Import: Now Admin-Only (All 12 Routes)
notes.description: Smart Import is the feature that ingests Excel spreadsheets and creates projects, cost lines, and revenue records from them. It is, objectively, the most dangerous feature in the application. It was previously accessible to anyone who could spell '/api/smart-import/upload.' We have now placed 12 Smart Import routes behind requireAdmin middleware. Upload, commit, rollback, bulk-commit, ignore-all-blockers (yes, that's a real endpoint name), allow-all, apply-prior-resolutions, assign-project, and project-matches — all admin-only. The import cannon now has a safety lock. You're welcome.

notes.title: Fuzzy Matching: Because 'Kuilsrivier Phase 2' and 'Kuils River Ph2' Are The Same Project
notes.description: Smart Import used to match project names with exact string comparison. If the spreadsheet said 'Kuils River Phase 2' and the database had 'Kuilsrivier Ph2,' congratulations — you just created a duplicate project with duplicate cost lines and duplicate revenue records. We built a fuzzy matching engine that normalises names, strips version suffixes, computes Jaccard similarity scores, and returns confidence levels. Above 85%? Auto-mapped. Between 50-85%? Flagged for review. Below 50%? Treated as new, but only if you explicitly confirm it. We also added SHA-256 hash-based rerun detection so importing the same file twice doesn't double your data. Again.

notes.title: Ownership Scoping: You Can't See What Isn't Yours
notes.description: Engineers used to be able to see every project in the system. Site PMs could browse tasks they had nothing to do with. Project Developers could read everyone's tickets. This was philosophically generous but operationally unhinged. We implemented backend ownership scoping: the projects endpoint now returns scope metadata per project, the tasks endpoint filters non-management users to their assigned or owned tasks, and My Work was already strictly user-scoped (credit where it's due). Full oversight is reserved for management roles. Everyone else sees their lane. The concept of 'need to know' has arrived.

notes.title: The Roles & Permissions Screen: Now Actually Useful
notes.description: The old Roles & Permissions screen was a single scrollable wall of tiny toggle buttons. It mixed navigation access with entity permissions in a way that made admins question their life choices. Section toggles lived next to delete permission pills. There was no way to know what was enforced by the backend vs what was just hiding a button. We rebuilt it into four tabs: Navigation (what the sidebar shows), Capabilities (what the role can do, with search), Scope & Limits (what data they can see), and Enforcement & Risks (what's actually secured vs what's just politely hidden). It's the difference between a control panel and a pile of switches taped to a wall.

notes.title: Role Comparison: Spot The Difference, Enterprise Edition
notes.description: Admins can now select two roles and see every permission difference between them in a table. Is the Site PM supposed to have delete access to lifecycle board entries? Probably not, but you'd never have known without clicking through 80+ toggles one at a time. Now you click 'Compare,' pick two roles, and get a clean diff. It's like git diff but for access control, and significantly less likely to make you cry.

notes.title: High-Risk Permission Alerts: The 'Are You Sure?' Tab
notes.description: The Enforcement tab now highlights every delete and override permission enabled for the selected role. These are collected into a 'High-Risk Permissions' card with red badges and stern formatting. It's the permission equivalent of a surgeon's checklist — 'You have granted this role the ability to delete procurement records, override quality approvals, and remove lifecycle board entries. Are you sure? Are you really sure? Have you consulted a responsible adult?' Roles with 3+ high-risk permissions get a shield icon in the role list. Consider it a gentle warning.

notes.title: Enforcement Truth: Honesty Is The Best Policy
notes.description: We added a panel that tells you, honestly, what is actually enforced by the backend vs what is just UI-level visibility gating. Backend-enforced features get green badges. UI-only features get amber badges. Known limitations are listed in plain text. We tell you about the missing row-level security, the endpoints that rely on frontend context, and the absence of rate limiting. This is not a sales pitch. This is a security disclosure. We believe you deserve to know what you're configuring.

notes.title: The Admin Control Center Knows Things Now
notes.description: The Admin Control Center has a new 'Permission Enforcement Coverage' card that shows: total backend-enforced routes (47), ownership-scoped endpoints (5), application-logic-only endpoints (2), recent access denials in the last 7 days, and recent import issues. It's a dashboard for your security posture. It updates live. It knows how many times someone has been told 'no' this week. The Enforcement tab in Roles & Permissions pulls from the same API. The data is consistent because we are professionals.

notes.title: Easter Egg Status Update
notes.description: Still there. Still undiscovered. It survived the security hardening pass because it doesn't have a write endpoint. It's read-only. It's harmless. It's also getting increasingly existential about its purpose. If a secret exists in a codebase and nobody finds it, does it bring joy? It doesn't know. But it's still waiting. Version 1.1 has not improved its social life.
